list.listitem: Cardinal symptoms of toxicity are hypotension, dysrhythmias, seizures, altered mental status, and coma. C
Serum levels of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) do not correlate with symptoms of toxicity or prognosis. C
Predictors of complications include altered mental status, seizures, respiratory depression, hypotension, dysrhythmias, and ECG changes occurring within 6 hours of ingestion. B
Patients asymptomatic 6 hours after ingestion are unlikely to have complications. B
Treatment of tricyclic antidepressant overdose is primarily supportive. C
Alkalinization with bicarbonate may be given for cardiac toxicity. C

background.definition: Patients who present with acute exposure to an amount of TCAs that exceeds the usual maximum single therapeutic dose or an amount equal to or greater than the lowest reported toxic dose should be evaluated for toxicity. Poisoning can be intentional, accidental, or iatrogenic. For all TCAs except desipramine, nortriptyline, trimipramine, and protriptyline, the lowest reported toxic dose is 5.0 mg/kg; for desipramine, nortriptyline, or trimipramine it is 2.5 mg/kg; and for protriptyline it is 1.0 mg/kg.

list.listitem: In 2004, the Toxic Exposure Surveillance System (TESS) national database of poison center calls reported more than 12,000 exposures to TCAs.
A total of 9% of these exposures occurred in children younger than 6 years and 32% of these exposures were unintentional.
Amitriptyline, either alone or in combination, is the most common antidepressant responsible for fatalities from poison exposure.
TCAs also account for more than 25% of overdose-induced seizures.
Intentional overdose.
Accidental or iatrogenic overdose.
Toxicity can be seen in patients taking normal doses, especially in older patients and patients taking other drugs, where clearance is impaired.

The symptoms and signs of TCA poisoning are due to its ability to deplete norepinephrine from neuronal presynaptic vesicles, block reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, block the fast inward sodium channels on myocardial cells, and block postsynaptic peripheral alpha-adrenergic receptors.
TCAs also have central and peripheral anticholinergic properties that contribute to manifestations of poisoning.
TCAs are mainly protein bound and inactive at physiologic pH. Hypoalbuminemia and acidemia can increase free drug levels.

TCAs are excreted via the kidneys after metabolism by the liver. They have high lipid solubility resulting in a large volume of distribution. Mean elimination half lives are highly variable because of delayed absorption from anticholinergic effects on gastric emptying, variable first-pass elimination, and the interference of other drugs on liver metabolism.

Monitoring of TCA levels in patients taking therapeutic doses is not recommended, but may be considered. If ordered, a serum sample should be collected after 5 days of therapeutic dosing and 1 to 14 hours after the last dose for a once-daily TCA or 4 to 6 hours after the last dose for a multiple-dose-per-day TCA.
Signs and symptoms of toxicity include anticholinergic side effects, cardiotoxicity (hypotension, heart blocks, dysrhythmias), neurologic toxicity, and pulmonary complications. C
Symptoms of TCA toxicity mainly occur within the first 6 hours after ingestion. C
TCA levels do not correlate well with symptoms of toxicity or prognosis. C
Patients with arrhythmias, altered mental status, seizures, respiratory depression, or hypotension within 6 hours of ingestion are at a higher risk of complications and require close monitoring. B
ECG changes such as QRS prolongation, QTc prolongation, R/S ratio >0.7 in lead aVR, and terminal 40 msec vector are good predictors of complications. B

Signs and symptoms of toxicity include anticholinergic side effects (blurred vision, dry eyes and mouth, ileus, urinary retention), cardiotoxicity (hypotension, heart blocks, dysrhythmias), neurologic toxicity (hallucinations, seizures, coma), and pulmonary complications (aspiration, ARDS, pulmonary edema).

Incidence of significant clinical findings after TCA overdose: 51% sinus tachycardia, 35% coma, 21% prolonged QRS duration, 14% hypotension, 8.4% seizures, 6.2% ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias, 3.6% cardiorespiratory arrest, and 2.2% death.
Sinus tachycardia is the earliest and most common cardiac manifestation.
Drug levels do not correlate well with symptoms of acute toxicity or prognosis and results of blood tests usually lag behind onset of symptoms.
An electrocardiogram should be performed on all patients.
The ECG abnormality which best predicts complications is a prolonged QRS interval (>0.10 seconds).
Prolonged QTc, T40-ms axis, and an R/S ratio >0.70 also predict a higher risk of complications. B
Experts recommend a blood gas assessment as an important part of an initial workup.
Have an index of suspicion for TCA poisoning in any patient with anticholinergic symptoms.
Obtain drug levels but remember that they often do not correlate well with toxicity, particularly in young and elderly patients.
Check an ECG for any evidence of cardiotoxicity and monitor for and treat further complications.
Immediate treatment should start with supportive care. C
Patients with evidence of cardiovascular toxicity should be given sodium bicarbonate to a pH of 7.55. C
Avoid classes IA and IC antiarrhythmics (quinidine, flecainide), which block sodium channels and could potentiate cardiotoxicity. C

Benzodiazepines are recommended for seizure treatment. The best antiepileptic for seizures has not been determined. Seizures should be aggressively controlled to prevent acidosis which can increase levels of free drug. C
Do not treat with flumazenil as it may provoke seizures even if concomitant benzodiazepine overdose is suspected. C
Immediate treatment should be supportive care with airway protection if needed, intravenous fluids for hypotension, and correction of hypoxia and metabolic and electrolyte abnormalities.
Induction of emesis is not recommended.

The benefit of gastric lavage or activated charcoal at reducing absorption or reducing complications is not well studied clinically. The decision to use these agents should be made on an individual basis, keeping in mind concomitant drug poisoning and interval time of presentation since ingestion.
Activated charcoal with and without saline gastric lavage have similar clinical outcomes.
For cardiovascular complications, alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is effective but the best dosing recommendations are not clear. The largest observational study alkalinized to a pH of 7.55.
Isolated case reports have used magnesium sulfate, glucagon, and vasopressin for refractory symptoms of cardiotoxicity.
Do not use antiarrhythmics that block sodium channels (classes IA and IC) as this could potentiate the arrhythmogenic potential of the TCA.
The best vasopressor for fluid unresponsive hypotension is not clear.
The best antiepileptic for TCA overdose-induced seizure has not been well studied, but benzodiazepines are recommended for acute seizure control.
Flumazenil is not recommended for patients with TCA poisoning as it may result in increased TCA levels.
Refer patients for psychiatric evaluation if poisoning was secondary to self harm or malicious administration.

Hospitalize patients who are symptomatic, younger than 6 years, have comorbidities such as epilepsy or cardiac arrhythmias or are taking medications that could potentiate the toxicity of cardiac arrhythmias, or have intentionally overdosed by coingesting other drugs.
Asymptomatic stable patients with no ECG abnormalities six hours after ingestion may be safely discharged.

Patients with one or more of the following within 6 hours of ingestion are at higher risk for subsequent complications, such as intubation: arrhythmias, altered mental status, seizures, respiratory depression, or hypotension. B

Patients who have none of these symptoms at 6 hours—arrhythmias, altered mental status, seizures, respiratory depression, or hypotension—are very unlikely to develop significant symptoms (0 of 28 in one stud and 0 of 102 in another). B
The best ECG predictor of complications is prolonged QRS (>0.10 seconds); other predictors include prolonged QTc, T40-ms axis, and an R/S ratio >0.70. B
Symptoms of toxicity are similar, but may present at lower dosages or even at therapeutic dosages.
